title: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Human Thinking” (from p. 620), p. 625. Scope: mechanisms of human memory storage and retrieval

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing imaging and behavior can test similarity-preserving retrieval and some representational predictions. They lack the cellular and connectivity resolution needed to establish the proposed random-layer hashing mechanism uniquely.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure neural population representations during encoding and similarity-based retrieval, testing whether successive transformations preserve near-neighbor identity as predicted by random fixed-input hashing better than learned attractor or predictive-coding models. Model-specific neural signatures would discriminate the mechanisms.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Macroscopic imaging cannot observe fixed random synaptic input sets.

Human memory includes multiple systems.

Many memory models predict similarity-preserving representations.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.4
data existence: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.38
analysis feasibility: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Behavioral and neural datasets can test whether memory retrieval is organized by similarity, which is the functional half of the claim. They do not resolve the proposed implementation, successive layers hashing random fixed input sets into codes stable under small changes. That mechanism remains one model among others consistent with the same public data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test whether successive neural populations, each depending on a fixed random subset of its inputs, produce codes that are stable under small input changes and that predict similarity-based retrieval. Such a layered random code matching behavior would support the mechanism; retrieval by similarity with a different circuit would leave the specific hashing claim unconfirmed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similarity-based retrieval is compatible with several circuit designs.

Present recordings do not resolve whether each layer samples a fixed random set of inputs.
